modalities.name: The Fitted Wish
modalities.tagline: Kind words, tuned until a guarded part of you can accept them.
modalities.whatItIs: The Fitted Wish is a coaching concept for people who find that loving-kindness phrases like 'may I be happy' bounce off or ring false. With a coach, you approach that resistance as a guarded part of you with its own reasons, and you rework the wording of a kind wish until it lands as true in your body.
modalities.coreIdea: A kind wish means little if part of you rejects it, so the wish is fitted to you rather than you being forced to fit the wish. Warmth is offered in the words, and at the dose, that a wary part can actually take in.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 50-minute session, you bring a self-critical voice or a stuck feeling, find where it sits in your body, and try a simple phrase of goodwill toward it. You notice how the phrase lands (it might bounce off, ache or soften) and, with the coach, rework the words, for example from 'may you be happy' to 'may you get a little rest', until something in you eases. You end by resting for a few minutes in whatever warmth came, and take one fitted phrase home to repeat for five minutes a day.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want more self-kindness but find standard loving-kindness phrases fake or hollow, and who like a slow, body-aware coaching style. It may also suit people already drawn to parts work or meditation.
modalities.cautions: Turning kindness toward yourself can stir grief, anger or a sense of unworthiness, and this is coaching rather than therapy, so people with trauma, severe depression or suicidal thoughts should work with a qualified mental health professional. The idea is untested, so go at your own pace and stop if it becomes overwhelming.
modalities.tweet: New concept: The Fitted Wish. If 'may I be happy' rings false for you, a coach helps you rework a kind phrase until the guarded part of you can actually take it in. Kindness that fits you, instead of kindness you force on yourself.

modalities.name: The Moving Knot
modalities.tagline: Track a stuck feeling moment by moment: is it really solid?
modalities.whatItIs: The Moving Knot is an imagined one-to-one practice that brings the close, moment-by-moment watching of insight meditation to the stuck feelings people bring to coaching. Instead of working out what the feeling means, you describe its raw sensations out loud as they shift, and a coach reflects back only the changes.
modalities.coreIdea: A feeling that seems frozen in place, like a knot of dread, is made of sensations that keep moving, and noticing this in steady company can make the knot feel less solid.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 50-minute session, you name something you feel stuck on and find where it shows up in your body. For about 20 minutes you then say aloud what you notice every few seconds ('tight', 'warmer', 'pulsing', 'fading'), while the coach mirrors the shifts and now and then asks whether it is the same as a moment ago. The session ends with ten minutes of silent sitting and a short talk about what changed and what stayed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who keep running into the same heavy feeling and want a calm, observational way to be with it, especially if they like meditation but find heavy feelings hard to sit with alone.
modalities.cautions: Close attention to a hard feeling can intensify it for a while and bring up memories, so people with trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should only try this with a qualified clinician rather than a coach. It is an untested idea and does not replace treatment for depression or anxiety.
modalities.tweet: An idea worth testing: The Moving Knot. You describe a stuck feeling's raw sensations out loud, second by second, while a coach reflects back only the changes. Tight, warmer, pulsing, fading. Maybe the knot is less solid than it feels.

modalities.name: Who Shows Up Uphill
modalities.tagline: Bursts of moderate effort, then slow minutes to meet your inner voices.
modalities.whatItIs: Who Shows Up Uphill is a proposed coaching session built on intervals of moderate effort, such as brisk uphill walking or steady cycling. Effort tends to wake up familiar inner voices, like the one that wants to quit or the one that pushes too hard, and the slow recoveries between bouts become a time to get to know them with curiosity instead of overriding them.
modalities.coreIdea: Moderate physical strain calls up protective parts of us reliably and in small doses, so alternating effort with recovery offers a repeatable, manageable way to meet them while they are still fresh.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up, you do six rounds of two minutes at a pace where talking takes effort, each followed by three minutes of slow walking. In each recovery the coach asks what you felt and which voice spoke up ('stop now', 'don't be weak', 'just one more'), and helps you speak from that part for a moment instead of arguing with it. The 45-minute session ends with a cool-down and a few minutes of stillness.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who notice a harsh inner drill sergeant or an urge to give up whenever things get hard, in exercise or in life, and want to understand those voices while moving their body.
modalities.cautions: The effort is moderate, but anyone with heart problems, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure should check with a doctor first, and you can slow down at any time. Strong feelings can surface, and since this is an untested coaching idea, not therapy, people with trauma or serious mental health conditions should work with a qualified clinician.
modalities.tweet: Here's a proposal: Who Shows Up Uphill. Short bursts of moderate effort, then slow recovery minutes with a coach to meet the voices that appear when it gets hard, like the one that wants to quit. Curiosity instead of a fight with yourself.

modalities.name: The Honest Huddle
modalities.tagline: Easy-paced group games, paused often to say what you really feel.
modalities.whatItIs: The Honest Huddle is a new group practice idea that mixes gentle, easy-paced team games with short pauses for honest speaking. Group play quickly stirs old social feelings, such as fear of letting others down, wanting to be picked or a flash of competitiveness, and the huddles let a trained facilitator and the group meet those feelings openly instead of acting them out.
modalities.coreIdea: Play shows how we are with other people faster than talk does, so the game becomes a live, low-stakes place to notice and name what it stirs. The honesty that self-refereed games ask for about the rules is extended to honesty about feelings.
modalities.whatYouDo: Eight to twelve people meet for 90 minutes on a field or in a hall and play simple passing games with a ball or disc at walking or jogging pace. Every ten minutes or so the facilitator calls a huddle, and each person says one short sentence about what they feel right now, such as 'I'm tense about dropping it' or 'I want to win and that embarrasses me', with no discussion or advice. The session closes with a circle where people share what they noticed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who still carry feelings from school sport or group life, and adults who want to practice being honest and present with others in a playful setting rather than a talk-only group.
modalities.cautions: Group play can stir strong feelings, and this is an untested idea rather than group therapy, so the facilitator should know when to suggest a therapist, and people with severe social anxiety or trauma may want individual support first. Running and catching bring a small risk of sprains and falls, so warm up, keep the pace easy and sit out whenever you need to.
modalities.tweet: What if a game paused every ten minutes so everyone could say what they actually feel? The Honest Huddle is a new idea: gentle group games plus quick honesty huddles, for anyone who still carries old feelings from school sport.

modalities.name: Found in Stride
modalities.tagline: Long, steady strides with a coach, listening for what settles inside.
modalities.whatItIs: Found in Stride is a concept for coaching done side by side on a long, easy walk or gentle jog. Walkers and runners often describe the mind growing quieter after 20 or 30 minutes of steady rhythm, and here a coach helps you notice that state, put it into words and find your own way back to it.
modalities.coreIdea: Steady rhythm can open a calm, roomy state that is easy to miss, and the practice sees it as a quality you already have, such as steadiness or trust, rather than something the exercise hands you.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and a coach walk or jog side by side for about 45 minutes at a pace where you can still talk, and the coach says little for the first 25 minutes. When you notice the mind settling, the coach asks a few slow questions, such as 'what is here now, and where do you feel it?', and invites you to speak from that state rather than about it, meeting any stuck feeling that comes up in the same unhurried way. After a cool-down walk, you choose one cue, such as a breath or a word, to help you find the state again on your own walks or runs during the week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who think more clearly on the move, find face-to-face sessions intense, and want a coaching style that draws on the calm of steady exercise rather than talk alone.
modalities.cautions: Build up walking or jogging time gradually to avoid knee, ankle and shin injuries, and check with a doctor first if you have heart or other medical conditions. Old feelings can come up even on a calm walk, and because this is an untested coaching idea, people with serious mental health conditions should also have a qualified clinician.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: Found in Stride. You walk or jog beside a coach for 45 minutes, and when your mind finally goes quiet, they help you notice that calm and find your way back to it later. For people who think best on the move.

modalities.name: The Carry Conversation
modalities.tagline: Carry a manageable weight and notice how you carry everything else.
modalities.whatItIs: The Carry Conversation is an untested coaching idea that uses loaded carries, walking slowly with a light to moderate weight in each hand, as a way into how you carry burdens in life. As you walk, a coach helps you notice where you brace, hold your breath or slump, and which inner voices come along with the weight.
modalities.coreIdea: The way your body takes a load is a live, felt picture of how you meet responsibility and strain, so you work on how you carry rather than on lifting more. The weight stays the same; what can shift is the bracing, the breathing and the stories around it.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 50-minute session, you warm up and then do several slow carries of about a minute each, with kettlebells, dumbbells or even full shopping bags light enough to hold with good posture. Between carries you stand still and say what you felt ('I held my breath like I always do', 'part of me refuses to put it down'), then try the next carry with a softer grip, an easier breath, or by letting the coach take one weight for a while. Each session ends with one carry done as gently as possible and a few minutes of sitting.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they carry too much, find it hard to ask for help or put things down, and would rather explore that through their body than in conversation alone.
modalities.cautions: Keep the weights light, breathe steadily rather than holding your breath, and get medical advice first if you have high blood pressure, heart problems, or back or joint injuries. Feelings about burden and responsibility can run deep, so if they become heavy, look for a qualified therapist, since this coaching idea can sit alongside therapy but not replace it.
modalities.tweet: Untested but intriguing: The Carry Conversation. You walk slowly holding a light weight in each hand while a coach helps you notice how you brace, hold your breath or refuse help. For anyone who feels they carry too much.

modalities.name: In Its Own Time
modalities.tagline: Let a calm animal choose to come closer, and notice what stirs.
modalities.whatItIs: In Its Own Time is a coaching session idea held with a calm therapy animal, such as a dog or a horse, and its handler. The animal is never called or coaxed: you sit or stand quietly with an open hand and let it decide whether and when to come close, while a coach helps you meet the hopes, fears and old feelings about being chosen or ignored that the waiting stirs up.
modalities.coreIdea: A guarded part of us opens the way a wary animal approaches, in its own time and only when it is not pushed, so waiting patiently for a real animal gives that inner patience a form you can feel.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sessions last about an hour in a quiet room, yard or paddock, with the coach, the handler and one animal free to move around. You settle, offer an open hand, and say aloud what you feel as the animal wanders, sniffs, comes near or walks away ('I want it to like me', 'I'm already bracing for it to leave'), and the coach helps you stay with those feelings kindly. If the animal does come close, you take in the contact slowly, while the handler watches its comfort throughout.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who struggle with trust, fear of rejection or a habit of chasing approval, who like animals and want a gentle, wordless mirror for how they reach toward others.
modalities.cautions: Allergies, fear of animals, bites, scratches and, with horses, kicks are real risks, so sessions need a trained animal and handler, short sessions for the animal's wellbeing, and freedom for you to stop at any time. Feelings about rejection can run deep, and since this is an untested coaching idea, people with trauma or serious mental health conditions should work with a licensed clinician.
modalities.tweet: A speculative practice: In Its Own Time. You sit with a calm dog or horse and never call it over. While it decides whether to come close, a coach helps you notice what the waiting stirs up, from fear of rejection to wanting to be liked.

modalities.name: Slow Gesture Inquiry
modalities.tagline: Four simple movements, repeated slowly to find what each means to you.
modalities.whatItIs: Slow Gesture Inquiry is a new practice idea that uses a few simple, flowing movements, like those of qigong, as questions rather than exercises. Opening the arms, gathering in, pushing away and sinking down each carry a felt meaning, and with a coach you repeat them slowly and pause wherever one feels charged, awkward or emotional.
modalities.coreIdea: Simple gestures already carry meaning in the body, so repeating them slowly can show what opening up, taking in or pushing away feels like for you today, without having to start from words.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a one-hour session, alone with a coach or in a group of up to four, you learn four slow movements and repeat each one eight to ten times in time with your breath. The coach then invites you back to whichever movement felt most charged, to do it even more slowly and say a few words from the feeling it brings, such as 'opening feels exposed'. You finish by doing all four once more, noticing whether anything feels different, and can practice them at home for ten minutes a day.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like gentle movement, find it easier to feel than to explain, and want a calm, body-based way to explore themes like openness, boundaries and receiving.
modalities.cautions: The movements are gentle, but adapt them to your body and keep up any prescribed treatment; old feelings can surface, so people with trauma, dissociation or a history of psychosis should get advice from a clinician and work with an experienced teacher. It is an untested idea, not a replacement for therapy.
modalities.tweet: Prototype practice: Slow Gesture Inquiry. Open your arms, gather in, push away, sink down, slowly, with a coach, and pause on whichever move feels charged. For people who can feel things more easily than they can explain them.

modalities.name: Whole-Self Suppers
modalities.tagline: Shared meals where you notice which side of you does the socializing.
modalities.whatItIs: Whole-Self Suppers is the idea of small, regular shared meals with a lightly trained host, where guests notice which part of them usually runs their social life, such as the entertainer, the helper or the quiet watcher. The aim is not deep group work but letting a little more of the whole person show up at an ordinary table.
modalities.coreIdea: Much everyday socializing is run by a few protective habits of self, often learned early, so a gentle, repeated setting where people can notice them and let other sides speak aims to make ordinary company a place to be more fully known.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to eight people meet every two weeks for a two-hour meal at someone's home or a quiet cafe. Before eating, each guest silently names the side of them that usually takes over in company, and during the meal anyone may tap a glass and say one sentence about what they feel right now, without anyone giving advice or analyzing it. The evening ends with a short round in which each person says what they noticed about themselves.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who socialize a lot but feel they are performing, or who feel lonely even among friends, and want company where more of who they are has room to show.
modalities.cautions: Choose a host and guests who feel safe, keep what is shared private, and step back from any group that feels pressuring. If social situations bring intense fear or low mood persists, this untested idea is no substitute for talking with a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: Feel like you're performing at every dinner? A new idea: Whole-Self Suppers. Small meals where guests notice which side of them runs the show (the entertainer, the helper, the quiet one) and let a bit more of themselves speak.

modalities.name: Bent Tree Walks
modalities.tagline: Slow guided walks where living things show growth without being improved.
modalities.whatItIs: Bent Tree Walks are imagined as slow, guided walks in woods, parks or along water, where a coach invites you to find a living thing or a feature of the land that matches how you feel inside. You might stay with a tree that grew around a rock, or a stream finding its way past stones, and let it show you how a feeling might change shape on its own, without being forced.
modalities.coreIdea: Living things grow around what happened to them and stay whole, which offers a felt picture of change by unfolding rather than by self-improvement.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and a coach, or a small group of two or three, walk slowly for about 75 minutes, starting with 20 minutes in silence to let your senses take in the place. The coach then invites you to let something catch your attention, such as moss on a stump or a twisted branch, to stay with it for a while and say what you feel in its company. The walk ends with quiet sitting, and later you can repeat it alone on familiar paths.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel worn out by pressure to improve themselves, find nature calming, and want a gentle, reflective outdoor practice with some depth but no heavy agenda.
modalities.cautions: Plan the route, check the weather, wear suitable shoes, carry water and tell someone where you are going, and watch for ticks where they are common. Old feelings can surface, so think of this untested coaching idea as a support alongside, not instead of, treatment if low mood or anxiety persists.
modalities.tweet: Something new to try on a walk: Bent Tree Walks. A coach invites you to find something in the landscape that matches how you feel, like a tree that grew around a rock, and stay with it. Change by unfolding, not self-improvement.

modalities.name: Room Around the Feeling
modalities.tagline: Let a hard feeling sit inside the whole field of your senses.
modalities.whatItIs: Room Around the Feeling is a guided practice concept that brings a stuck or painful feeling into contact with everything else you can sense in the moment. Instead of zooming in on the feeling, a guide helps you widen your attention, one sense at a time, until the feeling sits inside a much larger field of sound, light, touch and temperature.
modalities.coreIdea: A hard feeling tends to fill the whole screen, and letting the senses widen around it may help it take its true size: one part of a larger moment rather than all of it.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 45-minute session, seated with eyes open, you name a feeling you are stuck on and notice where it sits in your body. The guide then invites you to add, one at a time, the sounds in the room, the light on the wall, the weight of your body on the chair and the air on your skin, while the feeling stays wherever it is. At the end you notice how the feeling sits within this wider field and say a few words from it, and between sessions you can practice a five-minute version alone.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get swallowed by strong feelings and want a calm, sense-based way to be with them, without either pushing them away or diving in.
modalities.cautions: Attending to hard feelings can bring up memories or panic, so keep your eyes open and the freedom to stop, and work with a qualified therapist if you have trauma, dissociation or a current crisis. This untested idea is a self-care skill, not a stand-alone treatment.
modalities.tweet: Ever been swallowed by a feeling? A new concept, Room Around the Feeling: a guide helps you add sounds, light and touch around a stuck feeling until it is one part of the moment instead of all of it. More room, not more attention.

modalities.name: Felt Tone Coaching
modalities.tagline: Give a stuck feeling a sound, and hear it played back gently.
modalities.whatItIs: Felt Tone Coaching is an invented one-to-one practice in which a feeling that is hard to put into words is given a sound instead, such as a hum, a rhythm tapped on a drum or a few notes. A coach who plays simple instruments mirrors that sound back, so the feeling, or the inner part that holds it, can be heard without having to explain itself.
modalities.coreIdea: Some feelings are easier to sound than to say, and hearing your own sound mirrored back by someone else lets that feeling be received before it has been explained.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 60-minute session, you name what you feel stuck on, notice where it sits in your body, and let it make a sound with your voice or with a hand drum, chimes or a few piano keys. The coach plays it back softly, sometimes slowing it down or holding a steady note underneath, and you notice what changes as it is heard. You end with a few minutes of silence and one sentence spoken from the feeling rather than about it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who respond strongly to music or find it hard to talk about feelings, and want a gentle coaching space where sound can carry what words cannot. No musical skill is needed.
modalities.cautions: Sound can stir strong feelings and old memories, and this untested coaching idea is not music therapy, so people with trauma, depression or other serious conditions should work with a credentialed music therapist or another qualified clinician. Keep volumes low and stop whenever you need to.
modalities.tweet: Freshly invented: Felt Tone Coaching. Can't put a feeling into words? Hum it, tap it on a drum or find it on a few piano keys, and a coach plays it back to you, gently. No musical skill needed, just a willingness to be heard.

modalities.name: Whoever Arrives
modalities.tagline: Sit open, and greet whoever comes to mind with a brief wish.
modalities.whatItIs: Whoever Arrives is a meditation idea halfway between doing nothing and loving-kindness. You sit without choosing anyone to focus on, and when someone comes to mind on their own, whether a friend, a stranger from the bus or someone you resent, you offer them one brief, silent wish of goodwill and let them go.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill does not need a planned list: letting the mind bring people of its own accord, and greeting each one lightly, keeps kindness relaxed and shows you who is actually on your mind.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning basic loving-kindness phrases from a teacher or recording, you sit comfortably for about 20 minutes with no chosen focus, letting thoughts, sounds and daydreams come and go. Whenever a person appears in your mind, you silently offer one short wish, such as 'may you be well', and then drop any effort; if a plan, a sound or a memory arrives instead, you simply let it be. Afterward you can jot down who arrived and notice any patterns.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find structured loving-kindness practice effortful or forced, and people who like open, relaxed sitting but want a little more warmth in it.
modalities.cautions: Difficult people may arrive, and wishing them or yourself well can stir anger, grief or unworthiness, so keep sessions short and let a wish go if it feels false. Open sitting can bring up hard emotions or memories, so anyone with trauma, severe depression or psychosis should practice with a qualified teacher and check with a clinician before trying this untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New meditation idea: Whoever Arrives. Sit with no focus, and whenever someone pops into your head (a friend, a stranger, an ex), give them one quiet wish of goodwill and let them go. Kindness without the to-do list.

modalities.name: Snapshot Sitting
modalities.tagline: Do nothing, until a random bell asks what was just there.
modalities.whatItIs: Snapshot Sitting is a proposed meditation that combines letting the mind do whatever it does with brief moments of clear seeing. For most of the session you control nothing, and a soft bell at random moments asks you to note, in a word or two, what was there just before it rang.
modalities.coreIdea: Insight into how fast experience changes can come from honest samples of an unsteered mind rather than from constant watching, so the bell does the checking and you do nothing in between.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning simple noting from a teacher or guided recording, you set a timer app to chime softly at random intervals of one to four minutes over a 25-minute sitting. Between chimes you let whatever happens happen, daydreams included; at each chime you silently note what was present just before ('planning', 'itch', 'warm', 'traffic') and drop it. Afterward you look back over your handful of snapshots, or a quick written list of them, and notice how varied and changeable they were.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find continuous noting tiring but want more than open sitting, and anyone curious about what their mind actually does when it is left alone.
modalities.cautions: Open sitting can bring up difficult emotions or memories, and longer or retreat-style practice carries more risk, so start with short sessions; people with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first. It is an untested idea, not a treatment for mental illness.
modalities.tweet: A hypothetical meditation: Snapshot Sitting. You do nothing at all, except when a random chime sounds and you note, in a word, what was in your mind just before. A gentle way to see how fast experience changes, without constant effort.

modalities.name: Surge and Settle
modalities.tagline: Short bursts of brisk effort, then recoveries where you change nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Surge and Settle is an interval workout concept in which the recovery, not the effort, is the main event. After each short burst of brisk exercise and a few easy steps, you lie or sit down and do nothing at all: you don't time your breath, check your heart rate or try to relax, you just let the body come down by itself.
modalities.coreIdea: After effort the body settles on its own, which makes the minutes after a burst an unusually easy place to practice letting things be without steering them.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 5-minute warm-up, you do five rounds of one to two minutes of brisk effort, such as fast cycling, stair climbing or uphill walking at about 6 out of 10, each followed by half a minute of easy walking and then three minutes lying or sitting with no instructions. Whenever you notice an urge to control your breath, your heartbeat or your thoughts, you drop it. The session takes about 35 minutes and ends with five more minutes of doing nothing.
modalities.whoItsFor: Restless people who find sitting meditation hard to start, and exercisers who want their recovery time to rest the mind as well as the legs.
modalities.cautions: Brisk effort loads the heart, so people with heart disease, chest pain, fainting or uncontrolled high blood pressure should get medical advice first, and everyone should build up gradually. Get up slowly after lying down to avoid dizziness, and remember that this is an untested idea, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Surge and Settle is a new take on intervals: a minute or two of brisk effort, a short easy walk, then three minutes lying down doing nothing while your body comes down by itself. For restless people who find sitting still hard to start.

modalities.name: Nobody's Game
modalities.tagline: A park, some balls, no teams, no score: let the game happen.
modalities.whatItIs: Nobody's Game is an idea for group play with a few balls and discs and no teams, no rules beyond safety, no score and no leader. Whatever game emerges is the game, and the one shared practice is to notice when you are trying to control it, whether to win, to organize others or to look good, and to let that go.
modalities.coreIdea: Just as focus can arise by itself when you stop forcing it, play can arise by itself in a group when nobody steers it, which turns letting go of control into something social and moving.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to fifteen people meet for an hour in a park with a few soft balls and discs, and a bell starts and ends the session. In between, people toss, kick, chase, invent games, drift off and rest as they like, at whatever pace feels easy, and anyone who notices an urge to take charge or perform lets it go. Afterward the group sits together for a few minutes, and anyone who wants to can say what they noticed.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who miss unstructured play, people who tend to take charge or worry about performing in groups, and anyone who wants movement and company without competition.
modalities.cautions: Running and catching carry a small risk of sprains, falls and knocks, so use soft equipment, warm up, keep the pace easy and stop after any blow to the head. Open play can feel awkward or exposing at first, no one should be pressured to join in, and this is an untested idea, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Remember recess? Nobody's Game is a new idea for adults: a group, a few balls, no teams, no score, no leader. The only practice is noticing when you try to control the game, and letting that go.

modalities.name: Unwatched Miles
modalities.tagline: An easy walk-jog with no watch, no target and no pace.
modalities.whatItIs: Unwatched Miles is a new take on walking and jogging in which you hand every decision about pace to your body. There is no watch, no music, no distance goal and no 'good form' to hold: you set off walking, and the body breaks into a jog or slows to a walk whenever it does.
modalities.coreIdea: Steady aerobic exercise is usually managed closely, and dropping every intention to control speed, form or distance turns it into a moving version of letting whatever happens happen.
modalities.whatYouDo: Choose a safe, familiar loop and go out for 30 to 45 minutes with nothing to check, keeping a phone in your pocket only for safety. Whenever you notice yourself managing the run, such as speeding up to look fit, pushing for a distance or judging your stride, you let that intention go and carry on at whatever pace is happening. Afterward, you stand still for a minute and notice how you feel.
modalities.whoItsFor: Runners who have turned running into a numbers game, beginners put off by pace charts, and anyone who wants steady exercise that also rests the mind.
modalities.cautions: Even unplanned running can cause knee, ankle and shin injuries, so keep the total time modest at first, include rest days, and get medical advice first if you have heart or other medical conditions. If exercise starts to feel compulsive or goes along with disordered eating, talk to a professional; this untested idea is not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: An experimental twist on running: Unwatched Miles. No watch, no music, no distance goal. Your body decides when to jog and when to walk, and you drop any urge to manage it. For anyone whose running became a numbers game.

modalities.name: Just Enough Lifting
modalities.tagline: Lift moderate weights using only the effort each movement needs.
modalities.whatItIs: Just Enough Lifting is a strength practice concept built around dropping unnecessary effort. You lift light to moderate weights in a simple routine, let go during each repetition of any strain the movement does not need, such as a clenched jaw, hunched shoulders or a held breath, and rest with no agenda between sets.
modalities.coreIdea: Real effort and extra effort are different things, and lifting is a concrete, repeatable place to feel the difference and let the extra fall away.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week, you do four or five basic moves, such as goblet squats, rows, presses and hip hinges, for two sets of eight to ten slow repetitions, with weights or bands that leave a few repetitions in reserve. During each repetition you scan for tension the lift does not need and let it go, and between sets you spend about 90 seconds doing nothing at all. A session takes 30 to 40 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tense up or push too hard in everything they do, and lifters who want training that also teaches the body to relax under effort.
modalities.cautions: Learn the basic lifts from a qualified instructor, keep loads moderate, breathe steadily rather than holding your breath, and get medical advice first if you have high blood pressure, heart or eye problems, or back or joint injuries. It is an untested idea and not a treatment for any condition.
modalities.tweet: A proposed practice: Just Enough Lifting. Moderate weights, slow reps and one job: notice and drop any effort the lift doesn't need, like a clenched jaw or a held breath. For people who brace their way through everything.

modalities.name: The Grazing Hour
modalities.tagline: Sitting near grazing animals with nothing to do but be there.
modalities.whatItIs: The Grazing Hour is an imagined practice of sitting quietly near calm grazing animals, such as horses, donkeys or sheep, with their handler present and nothing to accomplish. You don't approach, feed or train them: you let the animals do what they do, and let your own attention do the same.
modalities.coreIdea: Grazing animals spend much of their day simply being where they are, and sharing that unhurried pace with no goal offers a living, wordless example of doing nothing.
modalities.whatYouDo: Up to four people sit on stools or blankets at the edge of a paddock for about 45 minutes while the animals graze, wander and rest. There are no instructions beyond safety: if an animal comes over, the handler guides calm contact, and if not, you simply stay, watch, doze or daydream. The session ends with a few quiet minutes before leaving.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find meditation too abstract or solitary, love being around animals, and want an easy, calming hour that asks nothing of them.
modalities.cautions: Allergies, fear of animals, kicks, bites and ticks are possible, so this needs a handler who knows the animals, a safe place to sit outside their space and the freedom to leave at any time, with the animals' welfare and routine put first. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for treatment if you are struggling.
modalities.tweet: Picture this new concept: The Grazing Hour. You sit at the edge of a paddock while horses, donkeys or sheep graze, with a handler nearby and nothing at all to do. No petting goals, no lessons, just an hour at their unhurried pace.

modalities.name: Echo Rest
modalities.tagline: Move slowly for a few minutes, then rest in the fading after-feel.
modalities.whatItIs: Echo Rest is a proposed practice that alternates short rounds of slow, simple qigong-style movement with a few minutes of standing or sitting still with no instructions at all. The movement leaves the body tingling, warm or quiet, and you rest in that echo without steering it until it fades by itself.
modalities.coreIdea: A short, structured movement gives open sitting something gentle to start from: the after-feel is vivid enough to rest in, and letting it fade on its own is the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn three or four simple movements from a teacher or video, such as raising and lowering the arms with the breath or slowly shifting your weight from foot to foot. You do one movement nine times, then stand or sit still for three minutes with no focus, letting the after-feel do whatever it does and dropping any urge to hold on to it, and repeat this with each movement for 20 to 30 minutes. It suits practice alone, morning or evening.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find sitting meditation hard to drop into, beginners and older adults who want something gentle, and qigong practitioners curious about the stillness after the form.
modalities.cautions: Adapt the movements to your body, sit down if you feel dizzy and keep up any prescribed treatment; unusual bodily or mental reactions are rare but possible, so anyone with a history of psychosis or serious mental illness should get medical advice and learn from an experienced teacher. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Can't just sit down and meditate? Echo Rest is a new idea: move your arms slowly with your breath nine times, then stand still and do nothing while the tingle or warmth fades by itself. Then the next movement. A gentle way into stillness.

modalities.name: Idle Company
modalities.tagline: Time with others where nobody has to do, say or plan anything.
modalities.whatItIs: Idle Company is a social practice idea: a regular, open-ended time to be with a few friends or neighbors with no activity, topic or plan. You talk if you feel like it, fall quiet if you don't, come late or leave early, and the only guideline is to drop the urge to fill silences or make it a good time.
modalities.coreIdea: Connection does not always have to be made to happen, and shared time with nothing to accomplish leaves room for closeness to arise by itself, the way thoughts settle when you stop managing them.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three to eight people agree on a standing weekly time of 60 to 90 minutes on a porch, a park bench, a garden or a living room, with tea or water and no screens. Nobody hosts, entertains or leads: people chat, sit in silence, watch the street or read, and anyone who notices themselves straining to keep things going lets that effort go.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find socializing tiring because it feels like a performance, people who feel lonely but are daunted by organized events, and friends who want an easier way to see each other regularly.
modalities.cautions: Spend this time with people who feel safe and kind, and step back from anyone hostile or controlling. If being with others brings intense fear or panic, or low mood persists, this untested idea is no replacement for talking to a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: A low-key new idea: Idle Company. A standing weekly hour with a few friends where nobody plans, hosts or entertains. Talk or sit quietly, come late, leave early. For anyone who finds socializing tiring because it feels like a performance.

modalities.name: Aimless Amble
modalities.tagline: Wander a safe green place with no route, goal or instructions.
modalities.whatItIs: Aimless Amble is an outdoor practice concept: you wander in a bounded natural place, such as a familiar park or wood, with no route, no destination and no instructions, not even to notice nature. You go wherever your feet take you, stop when you stop, and let attention drift between the trees, your thoughts and nothing in particular.
modalities.coreIdea: Most nature practices still give you a job, such as following a route or using your senses, and dropping even that leaves only you and the place, letting whatever happens happen while you move.
modalities.whatYouDo: Pick a safe, bounded green space you know, tell someone where you are, and wander for 45 to 90 minutes alone or with one quiet companion. Whenever you notice an intention to get somewhere, see something or make the walk worthwhile, you let it go and carry on, or sit for a while if that is what happens. The phone stays in your pocket, kept only for safety.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose walks have become one more task to complete, and anyone who wants rest that is neither sleep nor a screen.
modalities.cautions: Choose an area with clear edges you cannot get lost in, check the weather, wear suitable shoes, carry water and watch for ticks where they are common. Time outdoors can support, but not replace, treatment if low mood or anxiety persists, and this idea has not been tested.
modalities.tweet: Speculative, but simple: the Aimless Amble. Go to a safe park or wood you know and wander with no route, no destination and no instructions, not even to notice nature. Stop when you stop. Rest that isn't sleep and isn't a screen.

modalities.name: Stone in Hand
modalities.tagline: Hold one simple object, with no instructions on how to attend.
modalities.whatItIs: Stone in Hand is a proposed sitting practice in which you hold one simple object, such as a smooth stone, a warm cup or a piece of fruit, and receive no instructions about it. The object is an open invitation rather than an anchor: you may feel it, look at it, smell it or forget it entirely, and attention comes to it and leaves it on its own.
modalities.coreIdea: An assigned focus asks for effort and no focus at all can feel like drifting, so an object that is offered but not assigned gives the senses an easy place to land without asking you to stay.
modalities.whatYouDo: You sit somewhere quiet for 15 to 20 minutes with the object resting in your open hand or on your lap. If you notice yourself trying to pay proper attention to it, or to stop thinking, you drop the effort; if your senses drift back to the object you let them, and if they wander you let them wander. At the end you notice the object once more and set it down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find mindfulness exercises like the body scan too demanding, and people who drift too much in open sitting and want a gentle, physical point of contact.
modalities.cautions: Sitting quietly can sometimes bring up hard emotions or memories, so keep the freedom to stop, open your eyes and move, and see a trained teacher or therapist if that happens often, especially with a history of trauma. It is an untested self-care idea, not a stand-alone treatment.
modalities.tweet: Stone in Hand is a new idea for anyone who finds mindfulness exercises demanding: hold a smooth stone or a warm cup for 15 minutes with no instructions. Feel it, look at it or forget it. If attention drifts back, fine. If not, also fine.

modalities.name: Let the Hands Play
modalities.tagline: Play a simple instrument with no aim to make it good.
modalities.whatItIs: Let the Hands Play is an invented practice of playing a simple instrument that is hard to make sound bad, such as a tongue drum, a kalimba or a few piano keys, with no intention of making music. Your hands play whatever they play, you stop when nothing wants to play, and any memories or moods the sounds bring are allowed to come and go.
modalities.coreIdea: Making sound without trying to make it good, finish a tune or impress anyone turns music into a way of letting whatever happens happen, with the sound showing you, moment to moment, what that is like.
modalities.whatYouDo: You sit with the instrument for 15 to 30 minutes, alone or with two or three others who each have their own instrument and nobody leading. Whenever you notice an urge to play well, build a melody or match the others, you drop it, and silence is as welcome as sound. Afterward you sit for a minute in the quiet.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who were told they were unmusical, musicians who have lost the fun of playing, and anyone who finds silent meditation too empty but wants something just as open.
modalities.cautions: Sounds can bring back strong memories or moods, so notice how a session leaves you feeling, stop if it pulls you down and keep the volume comfortable. It is an untested idea, not music therapy, and no substitute for professional help with depression or other conditions.
modalities.tweet: Told you're 'not musical'? Here's a new idea: Let the Hands Play. Sit with a kalimba or tongue drum and let your hands play whatever they play, with no aim to make it good. Silence counts too. Doing nothing, with a soundtrack.

modalities.name: Warm Noting
modalities.tagline: Label each passing experience in a kind, friendly inner voice.
modalities.whatItIs: Warm Noting is a meditation concept that joins the clear seeing of insight practice with the goodwill of loving-kindness. You silently label each experience as it arises, such as 'hearing', 'thinking' or 'aching', but each label is spoken inwardly in the warm tone you would use with a friend.
modalities.coreIdea: The inner voice that observes experience always has a tone, and making that tone friendly means every moment of seeing clearly is also a moment of practicing goodwill.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning basic noting from a teacher or guided recording, you sit for 20 to 40 minutes in three phases: five minutes warming up the tone with a few goodwill phrases, most of the session noting experiences in that warm voice every second or two, and a few minutes resting in whatever is there. If the inner voice turns harsh or rushed, you note 'harsh' kindly and carry on. It can be practiced daily at home or on retreat.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators whose noting has become cold or self-critical, and loving-kindness practitioners who want to bring warmth into moment-by-moment awareness.
modalities.cautions: Intensive meditation, especially on retreat, can bring fear, panic or other hard experiences, and kindness toward yourself can stir grief or unworthiness, so start with short sittings and an experienced teacher. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician before trying this untested idea.
modalities.tweet: For meditators, a novel twist: Warm Noting. You silently label each experience as it comes ('hearing', 'thinking', 'aching'), but in the warm voice you'd use with a friend. Clear seeing and kindness in the same breath.

modalities.name: Warmhearted Intervals
modalities.tagline: Timed bursts of effort, each paired with short phrases of goodwill.
modalities.whatItIs: Warmhearted Intervals is a proposed workout in which structured bursts of moderate to hard effort are paired with silent phrases of goodwill, timed to the breath. During each hard minute you send a short kind phrase to yourself, and during each easy minute you send one to someone else, moving outward from loved ones to everyone over the session.
modalities.coreIdea: Kindness is usually practiced while calm, but life tests it when the body is stressed, so this rehearses generating goodwill while breathing hard and with a pounding heart.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 5-minute warm-up on a bike, rower or incline walk, you do eight rounds of one minute at about 7 out of 10 effort and one minute easy. On each out-breath of the hard minutes you silently say a short phrase such as 'may I be strong' or 'may I be at ease', and in the easy minutes you send 'may you be well' to a loved one, then a neutral person, a difficult person and finally everyone. The 25-minute session ends with a cool-down and a minute of standing still to feel what is there.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who already like interval workouts and want them to feed their inner life too, and people whose self-talk turns harsh when things get hard.
modalities.cautions: Hard bouts load the heart, so people with heart disease, chest pain, fainting or uncontrolled high blood pressure should get medical advice first, and everyone should build up gradually with easy days between hard sessions. Kind phrases toward yourself can stir grief or feel false, so let a phrase go if it does, and remember this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Kindness is easy when you're calm. Warmhearted Intervals, a new concept, tries it with your heart pounding: one minute hard, one minute easy, a silent 'may I be strong' on every out-breath and a kind wish for someone else in every rest.

modalities.name: Kind Rivals League
modalities.tagline: A gentle weekly game where wishing your opponent well is the practice.
modalities.whatItIs: Kind Rivals League is an imagined weekly game that builds goodwill toward opponents into friendly, easy-paced team play. At set moments in every game, players silently wish the person they are marking well, and a good week is measured by how much goodwill was practiced, not by who won.
modalities.coreIdea: Competition is where goodwill gets tested most reliably, so practicing kindness toward the people trying to beat you trains warmth exactly where it is hardest, while keeping all the fun of play.
modalities.whatYouDo: Ten to fourteen people meet weekly for 75 minutes to play a simple non-contact game, such as a walking-pace version of ultimate or another slow ball game. Before the start each player silently offers a phrase like 'may you play well and stay safe' to the person they will mark, after every point the scorer and the defender each send the other a silent wish, and at half time teams swap a few players so rivals become teammates. The session ends in a circle where each person names something they appreciated in an opponent.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy friendly competition but get too heated, people who want sport with a warmer culture, and loving-kindness practitioners who want to practice in a lively, social setting.
modalities.cautions: Even gentle games carry a risk of sprains, falls and collisions, so warm up, keep play non-contact, stop after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. Goodwill toward rivals can feel forced at first, which is fine, and this untested idea does not replace treatment for a mental health condition.
modalities.tweet: Idea: a sports league where the score that matters is goodwill. Kind Rivals League is an easy-paced weekly game where you silently wish the player you're marking well after every point, and teams swap at half time so rivals become teammates.

modalities.name: Widening Miles
modalities.tagline: Each stretch of an easy run carries goodwill a little further out.
modalities.whatItIs: Widening Miles is a concept that turns a steady walk or easy jog into a loving-kindness journey. Goodwill phrases ride the rhythm of your footsteps, and each stretch of the route is dedicated to someone further out: yourself, then loved ones, strangers, people you find difficult and finally everyone.
modalities.coreIdea: Distance becomes a map of the widening circle of kindness, so going further is felt as goodwill reaching further, while the steady rhythm keeps the phrases flowing without strain.
modalities.whatYouDo: You go out alone for 30 to 50 minutes at an easy, conversational pace, walking or jogging, on a route split into five stretches by distance or landmarks. On each stretch you silently repeat a short phrase in time with your steps, such as 'may you be well' over four footfalls, for the person or group that stretch belongs to. You finish by standing still for a minute and letting whatever warmth is there be there.
modalities.whoItsFor: Runners and walkers who want their regular exercise to carry a warmer purpose, and people who find it hard to sit still for loving-kindness practice.
modalities.cautions: Build up time and distance gradually to avoid knee, ankle and shin injuries, stay aware of traffic and your surroundings rather than drifting too far inward, and get medical advice first if you have heart or other medical conditions. Wishing difficult people well can stir anger or grief, so keep that stretch short if you need to, and remember that this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: A loving-kindness run, imagined from scratch: Widening Miles. Each stretch of an easy run is dedicated to someone further out: yourself, a friend, a stranger, someone difficult, then everyone. A quiet 'may you be well' every four steps.

modalities.name: Strong for Someone
modalities.tagline: Every set dedicated to someone, with a silent wish for them.
modalities.whatItIs: Strong for Someone is a proposed strength routine in which every set is dedicated to a particular person, along with a silent wish of goodwill for them. Getting stronger becomes a way of caring: you train to be able to carry a child, help a parent move house or simply show up with energy for the people in your life, yourself included.
modalities.coreIdea: Strength means more when it is for something, and linking each set to a specific person turns a solitary, numbers-driven routine into a structured practice of goodwill.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week, you do a simple routine of five or six moves with moderate weights, two or three sets of 8 to 12 repetitions each, with good form. Before each set you picture one person and silently offer a wish such as 'may you be safe and supported', then do the set with them in mind, and you can write their names in your training log next to the weights. Over the weeks the list can widen to neutral and even difficult people.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find strength training dull or too focused on appearance, and people who want their workouts to connect them with others even when they train alone.
modalities.cautions: Learn technique from a qualified instructor, add weight gradually, breathe steadily instead of holding your breath, and get medical advice first if you have high blood pressure, heart problems or eye disease. Wishing people well can stir grief or other strong feelings, and this is an untested idea, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Concept for anyone who finds the gym lonely: Strong for Someone. Every set of your strength workout is dedicated to a person, with a silent wish for them before you lift. Getting stronger as a way of caring, not just a number in a log.

modalities.name: Borrowed Warmth
modalities.tagline: Start kindness with a calm animal, then pass the warmth on.
modalities.whatItIs: Borrowed Warmth is a new loving-kindness session idea held with a calm therapy animal and its trained handler. Because warm feelings often flow most easily toward an animal, you begin by silently wishing the animal well while in gentle contact with it, notice where the warmth sits in your body, and then turn that same warmth toward yourself and other people.
modalities.coreIdea: Loving-kindness teachers often suggest starting with someone easy to love, and for many people a living animal right in front of them is the easiest, lending a real, felt warmth that can then be carried to harder places.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 40-minute session, you sit with a calm dog, cat, rabbit or horse and stroke it slowly for about ten minutes while silently repeating phrases like 'may you be happy and at ease'. Then, still in contact, you turn the phrases toward yourself, and after that toward a loved one, a neutral person and, if you are ready, someone difficult, coming back to the animal whenever the warmth fades. The handler watches the animal's comfort throughout and ends contact if it shows signs of stress.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to feel warmth toward themselves or others but feel it easily with animals, and people who want loving-kindness practice to feel less abstract.
modalities.cautions: Allergies, fear of animals, bites and scratches are possible, so this needs a trained animal and handler, good hygiene, short sessions for the animal's sake and the freedom to stop. Turning warmth toward yourself can stir grief or unworthiness, so go slowly; this untested idea can sit alongside professional care but does not replace it.
modalities.tweet: Some people find kindness easiest with animals. Borrowed Warmth is a new idea built on that: sit with a calm therapy dog, silently wish it well as you stroke it, then turn that same warmth toward yourself and other people.
